title: Quantum Computing
summary: A new kind of computer that uses the strange rules of the very small: qubits, superposition, entanglement and interference, how quantum computers are built, what they could do, and what they can't.

intro: Quantum computers don't just do the same things faster: they work in a completely different way, using the rules of physics that govern atoms and light. In this topic you'll explore qubits with coins and dice, find out why quantum computers live in fridges colder than outer space, separate the real promise from the hype, and discover the UK's plans to become a quantum leader.

pages.title: From bits to qubits

blocks.text: Classical bits

Every ordinary computer, called a **[[classical computer]]**, stores and processes information as **[[bit|bits]]**. A bit is always in one of two states: **0** or **1**, like a light switch that is off or on. Your phone's processor contains billions of tiny switches (transistors) that flip bits billions of times every second.
Qubits

A **[[quantum computer]]** uses **[[qubit|qubits]]** (quantum bits). A qubit can be 0 or 1, but it can also be in a **superposition**: a combination of 0 and 1 at the same time. When you **measure** a qubit, it gives a definite answer: 0 or 1.

blocks.caption: Bits and qubits
head: Feature
Bit
Qubit
rows: Tiny quantum systems: atoms, ions, particles of light or tiny superconducting circuits

blocks.text: Why "different", not just "faster"?

Quantum computers follow the rules of **quantum physics**: the strange laws that describe very small things like atoms, electrons and particles of light (photons). For some special problems, these rules let quantum computers find answers in ways ordinary computers can't. For everyday tasks, like word processing or watching videos, they're no better, and far less practical.
Quantum physics isn't science fiction. Lasers, MRI scanners, LEDs and the transistors in every computer chip were all invented thanks to understanding quantum physics.

blocks.title: Coins and qubits
steps: Place a coin heads-up: this is a bit storing 1. Turn it over: it stores 0.
Now spin the coin: this models a qubit in superposition.
"Measure" it by slapping it flat. Record the result. Repeat 20 times.
Count heads and tails. What do you notice?

q.q: How many heads and tails did you get out of 20 spins?
q.a: About 10 of each (results vary), because a fair spinning coin is like a qubit in an equal superposition: each measurement gives 0 or 1 with a 50% chance.

q.q: Explain one way a spinning coin is like a qubit and one way the model isn't perfect.
q.a: Like a qubit: it isn't heads or tails until "measured", and then gives one definite answer. Not perfect: a real qubit's superposition can be set to any balance and can interfere with other states, which coins can't do.

pages.title: Superposition and measurement
pages.spec: Describe superposition and measurement using probabilities
pages.summary: A qubit in superposition has a certain probability of being measured as 0 or 1. Measuring it destroys the superposition. With many qubits, the number of possible combinations in a superposition doubles with every qubit added.
pages.starter: Two light switches can be in four combinations (off-off, off-on, on-off, on-on). How many combinations for three switches? For ten?
sc: I can explain superposition using probabilities
I can explain what happens when a qubit is measured
I can calculate how many states n qubits can represent

b: A qubit's superposition can be weighted: e.g. 80% chance of 0, 20% chance of 1
Each measurement gives just one answer
Repeat many times to see the probabilities
Quantum programs run many times and look at the pattern of results
Measuring a qubit forces it into 0 or 1
The superposition is lost: measuring again gives the same answer
So you can't just "peek" during a calculation
Even accidental "measurement" by the environment ruins calculations (lesson 4)
1 qubit: a superposition of 2 states
2 qubits: 4 states; 3 qubits: 8 states
n qubits: 2ⁿ states
300 qubits: more states than there are atoms in the observable universe
slides.n: Starter: 3 switches = 8; 10 switches = 1,024. The difference: ordinary switches are in ONE combination at a time.

blocks.text: Superposition

**[[superposition]]** means a qubit is in a combination of 0 and 1 at the same time. The superposition doesn't have to be equal: a qubit could be set so that it has an 80% **[[probability]]** of giving 0 and a 20% probability of giving 1 when measured.
Measurement

**[[measurement]]** means reading a qubit's value. When you measure, the qubit gives a definite answer, 0 or 1, and the superposition is gone. Measure it again and you get the same answer. Because of this, quantum programs are usually run many times (called "shots"), and the results are combined to see the pattern.

blocks.title: Reading a weighted qubit
blocks.context: A qubit is set to have a 75% chance of 0 and a 25% chance of 1. It's measured 100 times (resetting it each time).
steps: Expected 0s: 75% of 100 = 75
Expected 1s: 25% of 100 = 25
The actual results will be close to this, e.g. 73 and 27, because each measurement is random.
blocks.answer: About 75 zeros and 25 ones. One measurement on its own tells you very little; the pattern over many runs shows the probabilities.

blocks.text: More qubits, many more states
Ordinary bits can only hold one combination at a time. Qubits in superposition can represent a combination of **all** possible values at once.

blocks.caption: Qubits and states
head: Number of qubits
Number of states in the superposition
rows: more than the number of atoms in the observable universe

blocks.text: This doesn't mean a quantum computer simply "tries every answer at once and picks the right one". When you measure, you only get ONE answer. The clever part is designing the calculation so the right answers become more likely (lesson 3).

blocks.title: Weighted coins
steps: Use the spinner your teacher gives you: three-quarters is coloured "0" and one quarter "1".
Spin it 40 times and record each result.
Calculate the percentage of 0s and 1s and compare with the expected 75% and 25%.
Combine results with the whole class. Do they get closer to 75:25?

q.q: Write your group's results and percentages.
q.a: E.g. 31 zeros and 9 ones: 77.5% and 22.5%, close to 75% and 25%.

q.q: Why did combining the class results get closer to the expected probabilities?
q.a: More measurements reduce the effect of random luck, so the pattern shows the true probabilities more clearly; this is why quantum programs are run many times.

o: It's lost: the qubit becomes 0 or 1

pages.spec: Describe entanglement and interference using simple models
pages.summary: Entangled qubits are linked so that measuring one tells you about the other, however far apart they are. Interference lets quantum algorithms make wrong answers cancel out and right answers add up, so the right answer becomes likely when measured.
pages.starter: Two magic dice always land on the same number, even in different rooms. How might you use dice like that?

b: Two qubits can be entangled: their results are linked
Measure one and you instantly know the other's result
Works even if they're far apart
Einstein called it "spooky action at a distance"
slides.n: Entanglement doesn't let you send messages faster than light: each result on its own is random. Keep this as a note for able pupils.

b: Waves can add up (crest + crest = bigger wave)
Or cancel out (crest + trough = flat water)
Quantum states behave like waves and can interfere

A quantum algorithm is a recipe of operations on qubits
It's designed so wrong answers cancel out
And right answers add up

blocks.text: Entanglement

**[[entanglement]]** is a special link between qubits. When two qubits are entangled, their measurement results are connected: in a common setup, if one is measured as 0, the other will also be 0; if one is 1, the other is 1. Each individual result is random, but they always match, however far apart the qubits are. Albert Einstein found this so strange he called it "spooky action at a distance". Experiments have since confirmed it many times, and the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for this work.
Interference

You've seen **[[interference]]** with waves. When two waves meet, they can **add up** (two crests make a bigger crest) or **cancel out** (a crest meets a trough and the water goes flat). Noise-cancelling headphones play sound waves that cancel out background noise.
Quantum states behave like waves, so they can interfere too. This is the real secret of quantum computing.
How quantum algorithms work
A **[[quantum algorithm]]** is a sequence of operations on qubits, designed so that:

items: The qubits start in a superposition of many possible answers.
Clever operations make the wrong answers **interfere destructively** (cancel out).
When the qubits are measured, the right answer is the most likely result.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Interference: cancel wrong answers, boost right ones
Measurement: read out the (probably right) answer

blocks.title: Wave maths
steps: Your teacher gives you strips showing waves as numbers (+2 for a crest, -2 for a trough, 0 for flat).
Add pairs of waves together, position by position. Which pairs cancel and which add up?
Play the "quantum maze": paths to wrong exits have +1 and -1 values that cancel; paths to the right exit add up.
Explain which exit the quantum algorithm would find.

q.q: What happened when you added a wave of +2, -2, +2, -2 to one of -2, +2, -2, +2?
q.a: They cancelled out completely to 0, 0, 0, 0: destructive interference.

q.q: Explain in your own words how interference helps a quantum computer find the right answer.
q.a: The algorithm arranges the calculation so the waves for wrong answers cancel each other out and the waves for the right answer add up, making the right answer the most likely result when we measure.

pages.spec: Describe how quantum computers are built and why errors and decoherence are major challenges
pages.summary: Qubits can be made from superconducting circuits, trapped ions, atoms or photons. They are extremely fragile: heat, vibration and stray signals cause decoherence and errors, so quantum computers need extreme cooling, isolation and error correction.

blocks.text: Colder than space

Superconducting qubits only work at temperatures a tiny fraction of a degree above **[[absolute zero]]** (-273.15 °C), the coldest possible temperature. That's colder than outer space. The qubits sit at the bottom of a **dilution refrigerator**, a tall gold-coloured structure often nicknamed "the chandelier".
Decoherence and errors

Qubits are incredibly fragile. Heat, vibration, stray electrical signals or even cosmic rays can disturb them, making them lose their superposition. This is called **[[decoherence]]**, and it causes errors. Today's qubits make errors far more often than ordinary computer bits, which limits how long a calculation can run.
Quantum error correction

**[[quantum error correction]]** groups many fragile "physical" qubits together to make one more reliable "logical" qubit, constantly checking for and fixing errors. In 2024, Google announced a chip called Willow on which errors went **down** as more qubits were added to the error correction, an important step towards large, reliable quantum computers.
Different companies count qubits differently, and more qubits isn't automatically better: the quality (how few errors they make) matters just as much.

blocks.text: Simulating nature

Molecules and materials obey quantum physics, and simulating them exactly on an ordinary computer gets impossibly hard as they get bigger. In 1981, physicist Richard Feynman suggested: "Nature isn't classical... if you want to make a simulation of nature, you'd better make it quantum mechanical." Quantum computers could one day help with:

items: designing new **medicines** by simulating how molecules interact
developing better **batteries** for electric cars and storing renewable energy
finding ways to make **fertiliser** using much less energy

blocks.text: Optimisation and more

**[[optimisation]]** means finding the best solution among an enormous number of possibilities, such as the best routes for delivery vans or the best timetable for a school. Quantum computers may help with some optimisation problems, though researchers are still finding out how much. They could also speed up some kinds of searching and machine learning.
The encryption threat

As you may have seen in the Encryption topic, a large, reliable quantum computer running **Shor's algorithm** could break RSA and similar encryption used across the internet. That's why governments and companies are already switching to post-quantum cryptography.
Separating hype from reality

**[[quantum advantage]]** is when a quantum computer solves a problem faster than any ordinary computer could. Researchers have shown this for some carefully chosen test problems, but not yet for most useful real-world tasks.

blocks.text: GPS signals can be jammed or blocked. Quantum navigation systems that sense tiny movements and changes in gravity have already been tested on ships and trains in the UK, and could keep planes and ships on course without satellites.
The UK's quantum plans

The UK's **[[National Quantum Strategy]]** (2023) is a 10-year plan to make the UK a leading "quantum-enabled economy". It includes billions of pounds of investment in research, businesses and training, a National Quantum Computing Centre in Oxfordshire, and research hubs at universities across the UK.
Careers

Quantum technology needs people with many skills. Physicists and engineers build the machines; programmers and mathematicians design quantum algorithms (often using Python with libraries such as Qiskit or Cirq); chemists and materials scientists find uses; and people in business, law, ethics and teaching help everyone understand and use the technology responsibly.
